opus-5.5.text:
Lean is really central to everything we do. The way I think about it is that Lean gives us a ground truth signal for reasoning. When a model writes a proof in natural language, you're always left with some uncertainty: is this actually correct, or does it just look plausible? There might be a subtle gap in step seven that nobody catches. With Lean, the proof either checks or it doesn't. The kernel verifies every step, so if the system produces a proof that compiles, you know it's correct.

That matters in two ways for us. The first is on the output side. If you want people to trust an AI system's answers on hard mathematical problems, or eventually on things like verifying software, you can't ask them to read through pages of reasoning and hope it's right. Formal verification means the output comes with a guarantee. You don't have to trust the model; you trust the checker, which is a small, well-understood piece of software.

The second, and maybe more important for how the system improves, is on the training side. Because Lean gives a perfectly reliable reward signal, we can do reinforcement learning at scale without worrying about reward hacking in the usual sense. The model attempts problems, the attempts that verify become training data, and the system gets better. It's a self-improvement loop where the data quality doesn't degrade, because everything that goes back into training has been checked. You can generate enormous amounts of synthetic reasoning data, and you know all of it is correct.

So Lean is kind of the backbone. It's what lets us move from a model that sounds smart to one whose reasoning you can actually verify, and it's what lets us keep pushing capability up without the system drifting off into convincing-but-wrong territory. Our bet is that this kind of verified reasoning is the path toward what we call mathematical superintelligence, and Lean is the foundation that makes that possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Lean is really the foundation of everything we do. The way I think about it is that Lean gives us something most of the AI field doesn't have, which is a ground truth that's completely verifiable. When our system, Aristotle, produces a proof, it's not a matter of a human reading it and saying, "yeah, that looks right." The Lean kernel checks every step, and either it compiles or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity, no hallucination that can slip through.

That matters for two reasons. First, for the end product. If you're going to trust a system to do mathematics, or eventually to verify software or reason about safety-critical things, you need to know the output is actually correct, not just plausible-sounding. Lean gives us that guarantee for free.

But the second reason is maybe the more important one for how we improve the system, and that's the training loop. The hardest problem in making models smarter at reasoning is getting a reliable reward signal. In most domains you're stuck with human preferences or heuristics, and those are noisy and expensive and they get gamed. With Lean, the reward signal is perfect. The proof checks or it doesn't. So we can have the model generate enormous numbers of attempts, keep only the ones that verify, and train on those. That's essentially how we do reinforcement learning at scale, and it's why the system can keep getting better without us needing a human in the loop to grade every attempt.

And there's a nice compounding effect. Every verified proof becomes new training data, and it also often becomes a reusable lemma that makes the next problem easier. So the library grows, the model gets stronger, and the problems it can attack get harder. Mathlib, the community library, was an incredible starting point for that, and we've been contributing back as well.

I'd also say Lean shaped the culture of the company. When your whole pipeline is built around formal verification, you stop accepting "it seems to work" as an answer about anything. That discipline shows up everywhere in how we build.

astra-6.text:
I think of Lean as the environment that gives us a precise definition of success. When the system proposes a mathematical proof, Lean can check whether every step follows from the assumptions. That’s a much stronger signal than having another model look at an answer and say it seems plausible.

That matters both when we’re solving a problem and when we’re improving the system. During problem-solving, we can try an approach, get feedback, and revise it. For training, verified proofs give us examples of successful reasoning that we can learn from.

The distinction is that Lean supplies the checking, not the mathematical creativity. The model still has to find the useful ideas—the intermediate lemma, the right construction, the way to break a problem apart. Lean lets us explore those ideas while keeping the final result grounded in something we can verify.

sol-6.1.text:
Lean plays two roles for us. The first is that it gives us a precise language for stating a mathematical problem and checking a solution. The model can propose a proof, but Lean’s kernel checks whether that proof actually follows from the assumptions. So we don’t have to ask another model whether an argument looks convincing—we get a very clear correctness signal.

The second role is in improving the system. When the model tries something, that feedback tells us whether it worked, and errors can help guide the next attempt. We can use successfully verified proofs as training data, so the system can learn from problems it solves itself.

The important caveat is that Lean verifies the statement you’ve formalized. You still have to make sure that statement captures the problem you intended to solve. But once you have that, you have a reliable foundation for exploring ideas and checking the results.

r001.rationale: The response says Lean’s feedback indicates whether attempts worked and that verified proofs can be used as training data.
